   828→def detect_apex_context(network_path: str) -> str:
   829→    """Check if a network contains APEX or KineFX nodes.
   830→
   831→    Returns:
   832→        ``"apex"`` if APEX-specific nodes are found,
   833→        ``"kinefx"`` if KineFX nodes are present but no APEX,
   834→        ``"none"`` if neither is detected.
   835→    """
   836→    if not _HOU_AVAILABLE:
   837→        return "none"
   838→
   839→    try:
   840→        network = hou.node(network_path)
   841→    except Exception:
   842→        return "none"
   843→    if network is None:
   844→        return "none"
   845→
   846→    has_apex = False
   847→    has_kinefx = False
   848→
   849→    try:
   850→        children = network.children()
   851→    except Exception:
   852→        return "none"
   853→
   854→    for child in children:
   855→        try:
   856→            type_name = child.type().name().lower()
   857→        except Exception:
   858→            continue
   859→
   860→        if "apex" in type_name or "invoke" in type_name:
   861→            has_apex = True
   862→            break  # APEX supersedes KineFX, no need to keep scanning
   863→        if any(kw in type_name for kw in (
   864→            "kinefx", "skeleton", "rigpose", "jointcapture",
   865→            "bonedeform", "rig_doctor", "configurejoints",
   866→        )):
   867→            has_kinefx = True
   868→
   869→    if has_apex:
   870→        return "apex"
   871→    if has_kinefx:
   872→        return "kinefx"
   873→    return "none"

   510→
   511→KINEFX_MIGRATION_GUIDE = """\
   512→KineFX to APEX Migration Guide
   513→===============================
   514→
   515→Overview
   516→--------
   517→APEX (All-Purpose EXecution) is Houdini 21's evolution of the KineFX rigging
   518→framework. While KineFX expressed rig logic as SOP node chains (each SOP doing
   519→one operation on the skeleton), APEX uses graph-as-geometry: the rig logic
   520→itself is packed geometry that flows through SOPs and is evaluated by an
   521→Invoke node.
   522→
   523→What Changes Conceptually
   524→-------------------------
   525→- KineFX: Rig logic = SOP network. Each SOP modifies the skeleton points.
   526→- APEX: Rig logic = APEX graph (packed geometry). SOPs build/edit the graph,
   527→  then Invoke evaluates it on the skeleton.
   528→
   529→Think of it as: KineFX is "rig as node chain", APEX is "rig as data".
   530→
   531→The key advantage is that APEX graphs can be inspected, serialized, shared,
   532→and evaluated much more efficiently than SOP chains. APEX graphs also support
   533→parallel evaluation and can be compiled for better performance.
   534→
   535→Common KineFX Patterns and Their APEX Equivalents
   536→--------------------------------------------------
   537→
   538→1. Rig Pose (KineFX) -> FK/IK Full (APEX)
   539→   - KineFX: rigpose SOP allows interactive posing of joints
   540→   - APEX: apex::rig::fkfull creates FK controls; apex::rig::ikfull creates IK
   541→   - The APEX versions generate proper rig controls with solve evaluation,
   542→     whereas KineFX rig pose was more of a direct manipulation tool.
   543→
   544→2. Full Body IK (KineFX) -> APEX FBIK
   545→   - KineFX: fullbodyik SOP with targets and pins
   546→   - APEX: apex::rig::fbik provides the same solver in graph form
   547→   - Targets and pins are wired as graph inputs rather than SOP connections.
   548→
   549→3. Configure Joints (KineFX) -> Character Definition (APEX)
   550→   - KineFX: configurejoint SOP sets rotation order, limits, rest pose
   551→   - APEX: Character definition nodes define the skeleton schema
   552→   - Joint limits, rotation orders, and rest transforms are attributes on
   553→     the skeleton that both systems read. The difference is how they are
   554→     authored and validated.
   555→
   556→4. Joint Capture Biharmonic (KineFX) -> APEX Capture
   557→   - KineFX: jointcapturebiharmonic SOP computes skin weights
   558→   - APEX: Capture operations work on the same weight attributes
   559→   - Skin weights (boneCapture attribute) are compatible between KineFX and
   560→     APEX -- you do not need to re-skin when migrating.
   561→
   562→5. Skeleton Blend (KineFX) -> Blend Transform (APEX)
   563→   - KineFX: skeletonblend SOP mixes two skeleton poses
   564→   - APEX: apex::rig::blendtransform blends in graph context
   565→   - The blend parameter (0-1) works the same way in both systems.
   566→
   567→6. Rig Wrangle / VEX (KineFX) -> APEX Graph Nodes
   568→   - KineFX: attribwrangle with VEX on skeleton points
   569→   - APEX: Custom nodes inside the APEX graph, or apex_editgraph
   570→   - Simple VEX operations (set transform, read attribute) map to standard
   571→     APEX graph nodes. Complex custom VEX may need a dedicated APEX subgraph.
   572→
   573→What Stays the Same
   574→-------------------
   575→- Skeleton representation: Points with name, transform, and hierarchy
   576→  attributes. Both KineFX and APEX use the same point-based skeleton.
   577→- Joint attributes: name (s@name), local/world transforms, parentIndex.
   578→  These are identical between the two systems.
   579→- Skin weights: The boneCapture attribute format is shared. Skinning done
   580→  in KineFX works with APEX rigs and vice versa.
   581→- Animation data: Keyframes on rig controls export the same way regardless
   582→  of whether the rig was built in KineFX or APEX.
   583→- SOP context: Both KineFX and APEX rigs live in SOPs. You are not changing
   584→  contexts (unlike the old OBJ-level bone system).
   585→
   586→Gotchas and Common Mistakes
   587→----------------------------
   588→1. Do not try to mix KineFX rig pose and APEX rig nodes in the same chain.
   589→   Convert fully to one system or the other.
   590→
   591→2. The apex::sop::fromkinefx node handles skeleton conversion, but it does
   592→   NOT convert rig logic. You must rebuild FK/IK/constraints in APEX.
   593→
   594→3. Joint naming matters more in APEX. The autorig and many rig components
   595→   expect standard naming conventions. Run rig_doctor after conversion.
   596→
   597→4. APEX graphs are geometry. If you merge or blast them incorrectly, you
   598→   destroy the rig. Treat APEX graph prims with the same care as any other
   599→   geometry data.
   600→
   601→5. KineFX wrangles that modify point positions directly may not translate
   602→   to APEX cleanly. APEX prefers graph-level operations over point-level
   603→   VEX. Consider using apex_editgraph to replicate wrangle logic.
   604→
   605→6. Performance: APEX rigs are generally faster than equivalent KineFX setups
   606→   due to graph compilation and parallel evaluation. However, the initial
   607→   build step (constructing the graph) adds overhead that KineFX does not

     3→
     4→Reads an APEX Invoke SOP, extracts the graph structure from packed
     5→geometry primitives, determines execution order via topological sort,
     6→and presents the result as HTML (for the panel) or plain text (for Claude).
     7→
     8→APEX graphs are programs stored as geometry (packed prims).  The internal
     9→structure is not fully documented, so this module uses best-effort
    10→introspection: it reads whatever attributes are available on the packed
    11→content and falls back gracefully when data is missing.
    12→
    13→All hou access is individually guarded so failures never break the trace.
    14→Outside Houdini the module imports cleanly and trace_apex_graph() returns
    15→an empty trace immediately.

   118→def categorize_apex_operation(type_name: str) -> str:
   119→    """Map an APEX operation type name to a category string.
   120→
   121→    Returns one of: "transform", "attribute", "math", "control",
   122→    "solver", "constraint", "io", or "other".
   123→    """
   124→    if type_name in _OP_TO_CATEGORY:
   125→        return _OP_TO_CATEGORY[type_name]
   126→
   127→    # Try case-insensitive substring matching for partial hits
   128→    lower = type_name.lower()
   129→    for cat, ops in _CATEGORY_MAP.items():
   130→        for op in ops:
   131→            if op.lower() in lower or lower in op.lower():
   132→                return cat
   133→
   134→    # Heuristic fallback on common suffixes/prefixes
   135→    if "transform" in lower or "xform" in lower:
   136→        return "transform"
   137→    if "attrib" in lower:
   138→        return "attribute"
   139→    if "solver" in lower or "solve" in lower:
   140→        return "solver"
   141→    if "constraint" in lower:
   142→        return "constraint"
   143→    if "input" in lower or "output" in lower:
   144→        return "io"
   145→

   203→def _safe_attrib_value(prim: Any, attrib_name: str, default: Any = "") -> Any:

   225→def _extract_graph_nodes_from_geo(
   226→    geo: Any,
   227→) -> Tuple[List[ApexGraphNode], List[Tuple[str, str, str]]]:
   228→    """Extract APEX graph nodes and connections from geometry.
   229→
   230→    APEX graphs store nodes as primitives with attributes describing the
   231→    graph structure.  The exact attribute names vary, so we probe several
   232→    known patterns.
   233→
   234→    Returns (nodes_list, connections_list).
   235→    """
   236→    nodes: List[ApexGraphNode] = []
   237→    connections: List[Tuple[str, str, str]] = []
   238→    seen_names: Set[str] = set()
   239→
   240→    if geo is None:
   241→        return nodes, connections
   242→
   243→    # Discover available prim-level string attributes
   244→    available_attribs: Set[str] = set()
   245→    try:
   246→        for attrib in geo.primAttribs():
   247→            available_attribs.add(attrib.name())
   248→    except Exception:
   249→        pass
   250→
   251→    # Candidate attribute names for node name, type, inputs, outputs
   252→    name_candidates = ["name", "nodename", "node_name", "label"]
   253→    type_candidates = ["type", "nodetype", "node_type", "callback", "op"]
   254→    input_candidates = ["inputnames", "input_names", "inputs", "inputconnections"]
   255→    output_candidates = ["outputnames", "output_names", "outputs", "outputconnections"]
   256→
   257→    def _pick(candidates: List[str]) -> Optional[str]:
   258→        for c in candidates:

   331→def _topological_sort(
   332→    nodes: List[ApexGraphNode],
   333→    connections: List[Tuple[str, str, str]],
   334→) -> List[ApexGraphNode]:
   335→    """Sort nodes in execution order using topological sort.
   336→
   337→    Falls back to the original order if sorting is not possible
   338→    (e.g. no connection data, cycles).
   339→    """
   340→    if not connections or not nodes:
   341→        # Without connections, put io:input first, io:output last,
   342→        # keep everything else in original order
   343→        inputs = [n for n in nodes if n.category == "io" and "input" in n.node_type.lower()]
   344→        outputs = [n for n in nodes if n.category == "io" and "output" in n.node_type.lower()]
   345→        middle = [n for n in nodes if n not in inputs and n not in outputs]
   346→        return inputs + middle + outputs
   347→
   348→    name_to_node: Dict[str, ApexGraphNode] = {n.name: n for n in nodes}
   349→    in_degree: Dict[str, int] = {n.name: 0 for n in nodes}
   350→    adjacency: Dict[str, List[str]] = {n.name: [] for n in nodes}
   351→
   352→    for src, dst, _ in connections:
   353→        if src in adjacency and dst in in_degree:
   354→            adjacency[src].append(dst)
   355→            in_degree[dst] += 1
   356→
   357→    # Kahn's algorithm
   358→    queue: deque = deque()
   359→    for name, deg in in_degree.items():
   360→        if deg == 0:
   361→            queue.append(name)
   362→
   363→    sorted_names: List[str] = []
   364→    while queue:
   365→        name = queue.popleft()
   366→        sorted_names.append(name)
   367→        for neighbor in adjacency.get(name, []):
   368→            in_degree[neighbor] -= 1
   369→            if in_degree[neighbor] == 0:
   370→                queue.append(neighbor)
   371→
   372→    # If sort is incomplete (cycle or missing nodes), append remainder
   373→    sorted_set = set(sorted_names)
   374→    for n in nodes:
   375→        if n.name not in sorted_set:
   376→            sorted_names.append(n.name)
   377→
   378→    return [name_to_node[n] for n in sorted_names if n in name_to_node]

   381→def _find_critical_path(
   382→    nodes: List[ApexGraphNode],
   383→    connections: List[Tuple[str, str, str]],
   384→) -> List[str]:
   385→    """Find the longest chain from any source to any sink.
   386→
   387→    Returns list of node names on the critical path.
   388→    """
   389→    if not connections or not nodes:
   390→        return [n.name for n in nodes]
   391→
   392→    name_set = {n.name for n in nodes}
   393→    adjacency: Dict[str, List[str]] = {n.name: [] for n in nodes}
   394→    predecessors: Dict[str, List[str]] = {n.name: [] for n in nodes}
   395→
   396→    for src, dst, _ in connections:
   397→        if src in name_set and dst in name_set:
   398→            adjacency[src].append(dst)
   399→            predecessors[dst].append(src)
   400→
   401→    # Find sources (no predecessors with actual connections)
   402→    sources = [n.name for n in nodes if not predecessors.get(n.name)]
   403→    if not sources:
   404→        sources = [nodes[0].name]
   405→
   406→    # BFS/DFS for longest path from any source
   407→    best_path: List[str] = []
   408→
   409→    for source in sources:
   410→        # BFS tracking path lengths
   411→        dist: Dict[str, int] = {source: 0}
   412→        parent: Dict[str, Optional[str]] = {source: None}
   413→        queue: deque = deque([source])
   414→
   415→        while queue:
   416→            current = queue.popleft()
   417→            for neighbor in adjacency.get(current, []):
   418→                new_dist = dist[current] + 1
   419→                if neighbor not in dist or new_dist > dist[neighbor]:
   420→                    dist[neighbor] = new_dist
   421→                    parent[neighbor] = current
   422→                    queue.append(neighbor)
   423→
   424→        if not dist:
   425→            continue
   426→
   427→        # Find the farthest node
   428→        farthest = max(dist, key=lambda n: dist[n])
   429→        if dist[farthest] + 1 <= len(best_path):
   430→            continue
   431→
   432→        # Reconstruct path
   433→        path: List[str] = []
   434→        cur: Optional[str] = farthest
   435→        while cur is not None:
   436→            path.append(cur)
   437→            cur = parent.get(cur)
   438→        path.reverse()
   439→        if len(path) > len(best_path):
   440→            best_path = path
   441→
   442→    return best_path if best_path else [n.name for n in nodes[:1]]
